snapshot.title: TNPSC Economy: GST & Fiscal Policy
snapshot.exam_hook: ⚡ TNPSC Economy Hook: GST: 1 July 2017. 101st Amend. 279A: Council. FM: Chair. Deficit: Borrowing. FRBM: 2003.

quick_notes.title: GST (One Nation One Tax)
quick_notes.detail: Implemented: 1 July 2017. 101st Constitutional Amendment. Indirect tax. Slabs : 0%, 5%, 12%, 18%, 28%.
quick_notes.explanation: GST stands for Goods and Services Tax, and it is an indirect tax, meaning it is collected by a seller from a buyer and then paid to the government, rather than being directly charged on a person's income. It was implemented on 1 July 2017 through the 101st Constitutional Amendment, which changed the Constitution to allow both the central and state governments to collect this single tax on the supply of goods and services. Before GST, India had many different indirect taxes like excise duty and sales tax, which created a complex system; GST replaced most of them with one unified tax, often called "One Nation One Tax." The tax is divided into different rates called slabs, which are 0% (for essential items like food grains), 5% (for items like packaged food), 12% (for items like computers), 18% (for most services and many goods), and 28% (for luxury items like cars and sin goods like tobacco). This system ensures that the same tax rate applies across the entire country, making it simpler for businesses to operate and for the government to collect revenue.

quick_notes.title: GST Council (Art 279A)
quick_notes.detail: Chairman: Union Finance Minister. Decision making body for GST rates.
quick_notes.explanation: The GST Council is a group that decides the tax rates for the Goods and Services Tax, which is a tax on the sale of goods and services in India. GST stands for Goods and Services Tax. This Council was created by Article 279A of the Indian Constitution, which is the specific law that set it up. The Chairman of the GST Council is the Union Finance Minister, who is the national government's minister in charge of money and taxes. The Council's main job is to make decisions about how much GST to charge on different items.

quick_notes.title: Fiscal Policy
quick_notes.detail: Government's policy regarding Revenue and Expenditure. Tool to control Inflation/Growth.
quick_notes.explanation: Fiscal policy is the set of decisions a government makes about how much money it collects from people and businesses (called revenue, mainly through taxes) and how much money it spends on things like roads, schools, and salaries (called expenditure). The government uses this policy as a tool to control two big economic problems: inflation, which is when prices of goods and services rise too fast, and economic growth, which is when the country's total production of goods and services increases. For example, if inflation is too high, the government can reduce its spending or increase taxes to take money out of the economy and slow down price increases. If growth is too slow, the government can spend more or cut taxes to put more money into the economy and encourage businesses and people to spend. This policy is managed by the Ministry of Finance and is separate from monetary policy, which is handled by the central bank.

quick_notes.title: Fiscal Deficit
quick_notes.detail: Total Expenditure - (Revenue Receipts + Non-debt Capital Receipts). Measures the borrowing needs of the govt.
quick_notes.explanation: Fiscal deficit is the total amount of money the government needs to borrow in a year. To find it, you take the government's total spending for the year and subtract all the money it earns without borrowing, which includes revenue receipts like taxes and non-debt capital receipts like money from selling shares in public companies. The result shows how much the government must borrow from lenders to cover its expenses. For example, if the government spends 100 rupees but only earns 70 rupees from taxes and sales, its fiscal deficit is 30 rupees, which it must borrow. This borrowing is necessary when the government wants to spend more on projects like roads and hospitals than it collects in revenue.

quick_notes.title: FRBM Act (2003)
quick_notes.detail: Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management. Target : To reduce fiscal deficit and bring financial discipline.
quick_notes.explanation: FRBM Act (2003) stands for the Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management Act, which was passed in the year 2003. This law sets rules for the central government to reduce its fiscal deficit, which is the shortfall between the government's total income and its total spending, and to bring financial discipline by limiting how much the government can borrow. The Act originally required the government to eliminate the revenue deficit (the gap when regular income falls short of day-to-day expenses) and bring the fiscal deficit down to 3% of the country's Gross Domestic Product (GDP), which is the total value of all goods and services produced in India. It also mandates that the government present a Medium-Term Fiscal Policy Statement to Parliament each year, explaining its plans for spending and borrowing over the next three years. The goal is to ensure the government does not overspend irresponsibly, which can lead to high debt and inflation, and instead keeps the economy stable.
